name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 22 June 1968

blocks.note: a bob was an old British shilling, a cheap sum
land is measured in acres

explanation.surface: A bargain plot of land bought to compete with a place called Beverley.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, the bumbling Bob Acres is a rival suitor to 'Ensign Beverley', the disguise of Captain Absolute.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Acres is the character who competes against the man calling himself Beverley for Lydia Languish's hand.

blocks.note: to dart is to bolt, run off suddenly
ahead, as in 'go on'

explanation.surface: People roaming about, darting forward.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton Wanderers is an English football club, so 'Wanderers' is the club's name rather than travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolton Wanderers is a Lancashire football club, so Wanderers stands for the town name that comes first.

blocks.note: surface reading: a favourite child who upsets its father
setter's reading: a pet dog, in nursery talk, whose noise suggests a disobliging bark at the master

explanation.surface: A spoilt favourite who has let their father down.
explanation.walkthrough: A child's word for a dog is the same as the noise it makes; the rest of the clue is the setter's playful nod to a surly bark.
explanation.definitionFit: Bow-wow is nursery language for a dog, the commonest household pet.

clue.text: Book not made on this race

blocks.clueFragment: Book not made on this race
blocks.note: surface reading: a race on which no bookmaker will take bets
setter's reading: a great work of literature, which shares its name with the big horse races such as the Derby

explanation.surface: A horse race that bookmakers refuse to offer odds on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a book' is betting slang, so the solver thinks of racing; the word wanted names both an enduring book and one of the five major English flat races.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic is a book of lasting acknowledged merit, and the Classics are also Britain's premier flat races.

blocks.note: surface reading: the geographical spring in Turkey where the river rises
setter's reading: in Genesis a river went out of the garden and parted into four heads, one of them the Euphrates

explanation.surface: Where the great river of Mesopotamia begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis chapter two describes a river flowing out of the biblical garden and dividing into four streams, including the Euphrates.

blocks.note: first meaning: the outcome or final effect
second meaning: Archie was First World War slang for anti-aircraft fire, which is shot upwards

explanation.surface: Someone asks Archie how things turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: Archie looks like a man's name, but airmen used it for anti-aircraft guns; the question mark flags the punning second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The upshot is the eventual outcome, and anti-aircraft fire is literally fire sent upward into the sky.

clue.text: Save the mark! Then save this first

blocks.clueFragment: Save the mark! Then save this first
blocks.note: surface reading: an exclamation of alarm followed by advice to rescue something
setter's reading: a German proverb, like 'look after the pennies', says save the small coin and the mark looks after itself

explanation.surface: An alarmed cry to rescue a target, then an order of priority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save the mark!' is an old oath, but here the mark is the German currency, and the hundredth part of it must be saved first.
explanation.definitionFit: The pfennig was the small German coin worth one hundredth of a Deutschmark, the equivalent of a penny.

clue.text: Female co-operative societies on the farm

definitions.text: Female co-operative societies on the farm

blocks.note: a hen is a female bird
co-ops is the short form of co-operative societies

explanation.surface: Women's co-operative groups formed in a rural district.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: the farm's houses where female birds live together.
explanation.definitionFit: Hen coops are the enclosures on a farm where the laying birds are kept together.

blocks.note: surface reading: soldiers backing the nine-day queen in 1553
setter's reading: a regiment sharing her family name, the Scots Greys cavalry

explanation.surface: Soldiers who stood by Lady Jane Grey in her brief claim to the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scots Greys were a British cavalry regiment known simply by the colour of their horses; Lady Jane Grey supplies the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greys was the familiar name of the Royal Scots Greys, a famous British cavalry regiment.

clue.text: This tide, in the affairs of men, is unpropitious

blocks.clueFragment: This tide, in the affairs of men, is unpropitious
blocks.note: surface reading: an echo of Brutus's 'There is a tide in the affairs of men' from Julius Caesar
setter's reading: Brutus says the flood leads on to fortune, so the opposite state of the tide brings misfortune

explanation.surface: A gloss on Shakespeare's line about seizing the moment when fortune flows.
explanation.definitionFit: The ebb is the tide at its lowest point, the reverse of the flood that carries one on to fortune.

indicators.note: about suggests letters turned around and moved into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A falsehood told about the novelist's elderly relative.
explanation.definitionFit: Aunt Léonie is the invalid relation at Combray in In Search of Lost Time, whose madeleine sparks the narrator's memory.

blocks.note: surface reading: the leading performers of a tightrope act
setter's reading: the constellation Libra, whose English name is also what a tightrope walker most needs

explanation.surface: The headline acts of a circus tightrope show.
explanation.definitionFit: Libra the constellation is known as the Scales or the Balance, and equilibrium is the essential skill on a high wire.

clue.text: A reedy fellow in no boisterous company

indicators.note: in tells us to look inside the following words, which keep the letters wanted among their company

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of no and the start of boisterous

explanation.surface: A thin-voiced man who does not fit among rowdy companions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reedy' sounds like a weak voice, but here it means playing a reed instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboe is a double-reed woodwind, so its player is a fellow who works with reeds.

blocks.note: surface reading: an owl's submission to a contest or its record in a book
setter's reading: the way in for a barn owl, the farm building's big door

explanation.surface: What an owl has entered in a competition.
explanation.definitionFit: A barn owl nests in barns, and the large door of the building is its way in.

clue.text: Such glory it is to be a climber

blocks.clueFragment: Such glory it is to be a climber
blocks.note: surface reading: the triumph of a mountaineer reaching the top
setter's reading: a twining garden plant of the bindweed family, whose name is this word plus glory

explanation.surface: A mountaineer's boast about the splendour of climbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Morning glory is a twining garden plant whose trumpet flowers open early in the day.

blocks.note: surface reading: a printing of George Borrow's novel by Oxford University Press
setter's reading: Matthew Arnold's Oxford poem about a student who left to roam with travellers, the Oxford version of Borrow's word-learning wanderer

explanation.surface: A university press reissue of Borrow's book about Romany life.
explanation.walkthrough: Lavengro means 'word-master' and is Borrow's scholarly hero living among Romany people; Arnold's poem gives Oxford its own such figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scholar-Gipsy is Arnold's Oxford student who joined the Romany, matching Borrow's learned wanderer.

clue.text: Doll Merrythought goes to a hop with a sailor

blocks.note: a hop and a skip are both small jumps
Jack, from Jack tar, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A woman called Doll Merrythought goes to a dance with a naval man.
explanation.walkthrough: A merrythought is a wishbone, and the toy wanted was made from a bird's wishbone and a twisted string so that it jumped.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipjack is an old jumping toy fashioned from a wishbone, so it is a plaything made of merrythought.

blocks.note: surface reading: an entire crew left bewildered
setter's reading: every one of the sailors out on the ocean, which is also an idiom for confused

explanation.surface: Every sailor on board is utterly bewildered.
explanation.walkthrough: Moidered is a dialect word, from Ireland and northern England, for confused or bothered.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means bewildered or lost, and taken literally it describes every sailor out on the ocean.

blocks.note: surface reading: a team hastily put together from whoever was available in Ireland
setter's reading: the legendary pair of felines from an Irish town who clawed each other until only their tails remained

explanation.surface: An improvised side made up of Irish players.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'scratch' team is a makeshift one, but here scratch is literal clawing.
explanation.definitionFit: In the legend, two Irish felines fought so fiercely that they devoured each other, leaving only tails.

blocks.note: surface reading: a cross-reference, as in a document's numbered section
setter's reading: the answer to 25 down is the poet known as the Shepherd of a Scottish Border valley

explanation.surface: A terse pointer to another numbered section.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet James Hogg was nicknamed after the Selkirkshire valley where he herded sheep, so this answer completes his title.
explanation.definitionFit: James Hogg, the 25-down answer, was famously called the Ettrick Shepherd after his Scottish Borders valley.

clue.text: Business premises where someone is usually stirring

blocks.clueFragment: Business premises where someone is usually stirring
blocks.note: surface reading: a busy office or workshop where somebody is always active
setter's reading: customers stirring sugar into their cups at a café

explanation.surface: A workplace where someone is always on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea shop is a small business serving cups of tea and light refreshments, which customers stir.

blocks.note: a canonised person is a saint, abbreviated St
Emma Woodhouse, Jane Austen's heroine, lives in the village of Highbury

explanation.surface: The family line of a sainted woman from Highbury.
explanation.walkthrough: Highbury suggests the London district or Arsenal's old ground, but here it is the setting of Austen's Emma.
explanation.definitionFit: A stemma is a family tree or genealogy, and in textual study a tree of manuscript descent.

clue.text: Some sort of leather, that's obvious

blocks.note: first meaning: the glossy varnished leather used for smart shoes
second meaning: plain, evident

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a material is plainly leather of some kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a high-gloss lacquered leather and, as an adjective, means clearly evident or plain to see.

blocks.note: first meaning: putting seeds and crops into the ground
second meaning: hiding false evidence on someone to incriminate them

explanation.surface: Farming practices that might involve cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: Planting is setting crops in soil, and also secreting incriminating items to frame an innocent person.

blocks.note: surface reading: a general domestic servant who does every household task
setter's reading: the biblical sister of Mary who was busy serving while Mary sat listening to Jesus

explanation.surface: A household servant expected to do every job.
explanation.definitionFit: In Luke's Gospel Martha is 'cumbered about much serving', and her name has become a byword for the busy housekeeper.

clue.text: The 19 Shepherd sounds more like a young sheep

blocks.clueFragment: The 19 Shepherd sounds more like a young sheep
blocks.note: surface reading: a herdsman whose name resembles his flock

blocks.clueFragment: sounds more like a young sheep
blocks.note: setter's reading: a yearling sheep, and the poet's surname matches that spelling more closely than the pig word

explanation.surface: A shepherd whose very name recalls one of his lambs.
explanation.walkthrough: The 19 refers to the 19-down answer; together they give James Hogg's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: James Hogg, Scottish poet and novelist, worked as a herdsman and was nicknamed the Ettrick Shepherd.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone sharing the poet's name
setter's reading: the next Poet Laureate, who shared his first name Alfred

explanation.surface: A person who happens to share Tennyson's name and title.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Austin succeeded Alfred Tennyson as Poet Laureate in 1896, so the two Laureates share a first name.

clue.text: Geniality one found in a good French home

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: bon is French for good
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Warmth and friendliness discovered in a fine French household.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonhomie is cheerful friendliness and easy good nature, a French loanword for amiable warmth.

clue.text: Ways of doing things that can be partly ornamental

blocks.clueFragment: Ways of doing things that can be partly ornamental
blocks.note: surface reading: methods with a decorative side
setter's reading: the word is the second half of a reduplicated term for small trinkets

explanation.surface: Techniques that partly serve as decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Knacks are skills or clever techniques for doing something, and the word ends knick-knacks, trinkets.

blocks.note: surface reading: a sluggish, inert chicken
setter's reading: a hen is a factory producing eggs, as a vegetable name might suggest

explanation.surface: A dozy chicken doing nothing much.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole clue read cryptically: a hen is the producing works for eggs; the vegetable is the aubergine.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggplant is the American name for the aubergine, while a hen is literally a factory for laying eggs.
